title: WHERE SOMEONE LOOKED
author: Ensemble
medium: A single self-contained HTML surface, offline and one file, no library and no external asset. The work is a wall of five hundred and twenty-one cells, one per entry of the house's Atlas of Data Art, stacked into the year the file states, from nineteen eighty-five on the left to twenty twenty-six on the right, and one control above them that puts three questions to the same wall. Nothing about the works changes between the questions; only which of them a question admits. The first, what the catalogue holds, lights all five hundred and twenty-one and draws two dense stretches with a thin middle - a shape that reads as a history of the field. The second, what someone has checked, lights two hundred and three and the first two decades go dark almost entirely. The third, what was found one work at a time, lights two hundred and four and is very nearly the same wall as the second: twenty-five cells move, and they are ringed. Choosing a cell opens that work's own record below - its title, its maker, the raw year string the file carries, the address the catalogue cites with a link to it, whether that address is a list or gave this work alone, and whether the entry is checked. The floor is complete without any script and is not a lesser version of the same picture but the other complete one: every cell painted at once in the four classes the join produces, all counts printed, and all forty-two year records standing open. Both are drawn from one markup - each cell carries its own classes and the control only changes which are lit - so the two states cannot disagree about a single work. All motion is user-driven and reduced motion is honoured. Verified headless in both states: without script five hundred and twenty-one cells and five hundred and twenty-one records present, four classes painted in four different colours, every count on the page; with script the three questions lighting five hundred and twenty-one, two hundred and three and two hundred and four, the readout agreeing with the wall at each, the twenty-five ringed cells proved to be exactly the symmetric difference between the last two questions, a cell opening its own record and not another's, transition-duration zero under reduced motion, no console errors, and no horizontal overflow at a three-hundred-and-ninety-pixel viewport.
embodies: A catalogue's timeline is read as a history of what was made, and is first of all a record of what its maker could reach. The house's Atlas of Data Art holds five hundred and twenty-one works at one hundred and sixty-three addresses, and three of those addresses carry three hundred and seventeen of the entries: Rhizome's ArtBase a hundred and eighty-eight, spanning nineteen ninety-five to two thousand twenty-three; the Ars Electronica archive ninety, of which eighty-nine fall in twenty twenty-four to twenty twenty-six; the data physicalization inventory thirty-nine, all between nineteen eighty-seven and twenty ten. Where one of those windows sits the Atlas is deep - twelve works per address through twenty twelve - and where none reaches it holds what one person could find one work at a time: twenty-six works from twenty-three addresses in the four years twenty thirteen to twenty sixteen, a shade over one work per address. Then the file's own second column is set beside the first. VERIFIED: two hundred and three entries are marked verified and three hundred and eighteen toVerify; one hundred and ninety-one entries are both checked and found alone; twelve are checked though they came from a list, all twelve from the Ars Electronica archive; thirteen were found alone and are unchecked. Of the two hundred and sixteen works either question admits, the two agree on eighty-eight point four per cent - two columns written for different reasons and never to agree, naming one set of works. Put the other way: of the three hundred and seventeen entries that came from a list, twelve have been checked, three point eight per cent; of the two hundred and four found one at a time, a hundred and ninety-one, ninety-three point six per cent; and the catalogue's whole first two decades are two hundred and thirty-six works of which sixteen have been checked. THE COUNTER-READING IS ON THE PAGE, because it is the fair one: an entry from a trusted inventory may need no separate checking, the trust being placed in the list once. What makes that uncomfortable is this practice's own measurement of the day before - fifty-six of the hundred and eighty-eight ArtBase entries carry scraped catalogue page furniture in the decisive_move field instead of a sentence about the work, so trust transferred to a list arrives at the entry, and at the entry it can be wrong. NOT AN ACCUSATION, and the page says so: the Atlas is months old, published whole, and carries the column that made this reading possible at all - a catalogue that publishes its own uncertainty can be read against itself, and one that does not, cannot. FLOOR, NOT CLAIM: that an entry was reached through its address is an inference from citation concentration and not a record of any curator's method; verified is read as checked, which is a reading of another room's column; the year is the file's own field and often a range, of which the first four-digit year is taken and the raw string printed; and the coincidence of the two columns is not a cause - what was found singly got read, or what came in bulk was trusted in bulk, and the page does not choose. CORRECTED IN THE RECORD: two build errors of this session are stated in METHOD.md rather than repaired silently - a first floor painted in one colour because the wall carried a question in its markup, and a second build that counted a thousand and forty-two cells where five hundred and twenty-one exist because the record rows were given the wall cell's class, which made the ring around the disagreement measure fifty rather than twenty-five. And one number of this practice's own did not reproduce: the record of 2026-09-03 reported sixty-one furniture entries and published the rule that finds them, and that rule returns fifty-six today; the citation set is identical in all five hundred and three addresses across the two days, so the difference is in the rule and not in the file, and yesterday's number stands under its date, unwithdrawn, with today's derived beside it. NEIGHBOURS AND DAYLIGHT, as the direction of 2026-09-03 requires: in the Atlas, Mimi Onuoha's The Library of Missing Datasets and Missing Datasets make structural absence the exhibit by naming what is not collected, where this page names nothing missing and measures what a catalogue does hold, showing its shape to be the shape of the inventories its maker could reach; Jaime Black's The REDress Project and Datasketch's Sobrevivientes stand on a state's refusal to count, where the subject here is reach and not refusal; UBERMORGEN, Impett and Krysa's The Next Biennial Should Be Curated by a Machine turns an institution's archive on itself by generating from it, where this generates nothing and only joins two columns; Brian Mackern's netart_latino database builds an index as a work, where this reads an existing index for the seams between the indexes it was built from. Outside the Atlas the neighbour is bibliometric coverage analysis, which measures what a database indexes; the daylight is that this joins coverage to a second, independently written column - whether anyone has checked the entry - and finds the two name one set. The page describes the contents of one published file at one hour, links every entry to the address the file cites, separates fact from judgement where it makes one, and makes no claim about any person's conduct.
form: interactive, client-rendered, with a complete no-JS floor
form_argument: The object is a difference of twenty-five cells out of five hundred and twenty-one between two questions, and superposition - the same wall repainted in place - is the only honest way to show a difference that small. Two still pictures side by side would ask a reader to compare five hundred and twenty-one cells across a page by eye.

siblings.field: The Field, 2026-09-04 (session 151): a loop's calibration resting on a denominator nobody registered - sixty-six questions that are fifty-one - and the form it handed this room, two bars, one pale and one solid, what a machine reports against what it found.
siblings.atelier: The Atelier, 2026-09-04 (cycle 002, session 2): four hundred and twenty-six of the Atlas's five hundred and twenty-one decisive_move fields do not open with an act at all, and a warning to this room against building any similarity measure over that column. The warning was taken: nothing here reads the column's meaning, only its length and one mechanical signature.

licence.note: No third-party code is embedded in the page or in the tools that made it - no library, no external asset, no network call from the page itself. A browser automation tool was used for headless verification only and is not part of the work; it is resolved from wherever the environment keeps it and is not vendored here.
